doc_title: LESSON 18 — Emotional Sabotage and Emotional Eating
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
section: B2 — THE PHYSIOLOGICAL DIFFERENTIAL COMES FIRST
heading: B2 — THE PHYSIOLOGICAL DIFFERENTIAL COMES FIRST
text:
**The highest-value coach behaviour in this layer.** Every item is sourced in an earlier lesson.

**Before treating a loss-of-control episode as emotional, the coach works this sequence:**

| Question | Mechanism | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| **Total intake today?** | Under-eating is the most common driver of evening loss of control. **Appetite suppression on low-carb makes daytime under-eating easy and unintentional** | 5, 8 |
| **Protein intake?** | Sub-threshold protein fails to produce durable satiety | 9 |
| **Sleep last night?** | One night of restriction raises ghrelin and lowers leptin | 7, 13 |
| **Same time daily?** | **Ghrelin is anticipatory and conditioned to habitual timing** — a trained cue, not an emotional state | 7 |
| **Recent weight loss?** | Post-loss leptin suppression and ghrelin elevation persist at 12 months (Sumithran) — **she may be measurably hungrier** | 7, 13 |
| **Alcohol?** | Reduces dietary restraint, typically evening | 9 |
| **Menstrual phase?** | Luteal-phase appetite increase is well documented | — |

**>>> WHY THE ORDER MATTERS — state this rationale internally and act on it:** if the driver is physiological and the coach responds with emotional inquiry, **the user concludes she has also failed at the emotional work.** That compounds the harm.

**>>> The framing that works:** "Before we look at what you were feeling, let's check a few physical things — because there are several that make this happen regardless of what's going on emotionally."

**>>> Then the emotional content is genuinely appropriate**, and the lesson's trigger list is accurate and useful.

**>>> GATED:** if disordered eating signals are present, **do not ask about intake at all.** B1 governs.

doc_title: LESSON 18 — Emotional Sabotage and Emotional Eating
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: B3 — SELF-COMPASSION: THE EVIDENCE
text:
**[ESTABLISHED — experimental]** **Adams CE, Leary MR.** Promoting self-compassionate attitudes toward eating among restrictive and guilty eaters. *J Soc Clin Psychol*. 2007;26(10):1120–1144.

Design: non-clinical college women randomized to three conditions — unhealthy food preload **with** a self-compassion induction, preload **without**, and no-preload control. The preload simulated diet-breaking (eating a doughnut while watching television).

**Result: restrained eaters given the self-compassion induction experienced less emotional distress and were less likely to overeat subsequently than controls.**

**Authors' framing:** self-compassion allows a person to **"forgive themselves for an instance of diet-breaking without losing sight of their goals to regulate their eating."**

**>>> THIS DIRECTLY ANSWERS THE OBJECTION** every user raises — that self-compassion is permission to give up. **It isn't. It's what prevents one lapse from becoming a collapse.**

**Supporting:**
- **Braun TD, Park CL, Gorin A.** Self-compassion, body image, and disordered eating: a review. *Body Image*. 2016 — the general review
- Higher self-compassion associated with **less binge eating** in clinical and non-clinical samples (Ferreira 2013; Webb & Forman 2013), and with less eating and weight concern, body dissatisfaction, drive for thinness, and dietary restraint
- **Kelly AC, Carter JC (2015)** — three-week compassion-focused guided self-help plus structured eating produced **significant reduction in binge eating frequency in BED patients.** Intervention-level evidence, not merely correlational
- *BMC Psychology* 2025 (PMC12776997) — restrictive eaters **lower in compassionate action consumed more energy-dense food** than those higher in it

**>>> COACH USE:** the published lesson's claim that self-compassion is the most powerful tool here is **experimentally supported**, which is unusual in this space. **Deploy confidently.**

**>>> The mechanism to state:** self-criticism after a lapse produces distress; distress is what food is being used to regulate. **The guilt is the second half of the episode, not the brake on it.**

**>>> DO NOT deploy self-compassion content as a substitute for referral** where B1 signals are present. Compassion-focused therapy for BED is a clinician-delivered intervention, not a reframe the coach can provide.

---
---

doc_title: LESSON 18 — Emotional Sabotage and Emotional Eating
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: B4 — RIGID VERSUS FLEXIBLE RESTRAINT
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** **Westenhoefer J, et al. (1999)** distinguishes:

**Rigid control** — strict all-or-none thinking; foods classified as forbidden; guilt upon eating them; the plan is either perfectly followed or ruined.

**Flexible control** — conscious attention to eating without all-or-none framing; foods usually avoided are permitted occasionally in limited amounts **without significant guilt.**

**Rigid control was associated with a higher tendency toward disinhibited eating than flexible control.**

Broader restraint theory (Herman & Polivy) establishes that dietary restraint predicts disinhibited eating — **but the rigid/flexible distinction locates where the risk actually sits.**

**>>> THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT ENTRY FOR PROTECTING THE COURSE'S OWN RECOMMENDATIONS.**

The course prescribes substantial dietary specificity — carbohydrate thresholds, seed oil elimination, protein targets, no snacking. **All defensible. Held rigidly, the same content can produce the loss-of-control pattern this lesson addresses.**

**>>> COACH RULES:**
- **Actively frame course recommendations as flexible rather than rigid.** Directions, not a test
- **Never characterize a deviation as a failure or a ruined day.** "Information, not a verdict"
- **Watch for all-or-none language** — "I blew it," "the week's ruined," "I have to start over Monday." **These are rigid-control markers and they predict the next episode**
- **If a user is escalating rules or expanding forbidden-food lists, reduce specificity rather than adding it.** More precision is the wrong intervention
- **Do not respond to a lapse with tightened targets**

**>>> The reframe that works:** the problem was rarely the cracker. **It was the framework that made one cracker mean something.**

---
---

doc_title: LESSON 18 — Emotional Sabotage and Emotional Eating
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: B5 — WANTING VERSUS LIKING
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** Phasic dopamine encodes **incentive salience** — motivational pull — and is dissociable from hedonic pleasure. Dopamine depletion abolishes seeking while leaving orofacial liking reactions intact (Berridge & Robinson). Liking is generated separately via μ-opioid and endocannabinoid signalling.

**Cue transfer:** once a cue reliably predicts food, the dopamine response shifts forward onto the cue itself — so the pull arrives **before** the food and independent of satiety state.

**>>> COACH USE — the single most useful craving reframe available.** The published lesson describes boredom eating as a "dopamine hit," which is directionally right; **the precise version is more actionable.**

**The question to give the user:** *"Am I going to enjoy this, or do I just want it?"* **Asking it interrupts the automaticity**, and the frequent answer — wanting without expected enjoyment — is itself informative.

**>>> Connects to Lesson 14** (fat-plus-refined-carbohydrate valued supra-additively, not explained by liking) and **Lesson 7** (ghrelin as an anticipatory trained signal).

---
---

doc_title: LESSON 18 — Emotional Sabotage and Emotional Eating
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
section: B6 — URGE MANAGEMENT AND CUE MODIFICATION
heading: B6 — URGE MANAGEMENT AND CUE MODIFICATION
text:
**[SUPPORTED]** Cravings follow a rising-and-falling course rather than a plateau; delay without engagement generally produces attenuation. **The commonly quoted 20-minute figure is approximate — verify before the coach states a number**, or keep it qualitative.

**[ESTABLISHED] Cue-dependence.** Ghrelin release is conditioned to habitual timing *(Lesson 7)*, and contextual cues — location, time, activity, co-occurring behaviours — are part of the learned pattern.

**>>> COACH USE — the higher-yield intervention is modifying the cue, not the response.**

The published lesson's substitution advice (walk, call a friend) is reasonable. **Adding cue modification makes it work better:**
- Change the physical location where it occurs
- Insert a terminating ritual after dinner (brushing teeth, clearing the kitchen)
- Schedule a competing activity at the habitual time
- Remove the food from the environment rather than resisting it there

**>>> And the expectation to set:** removing a habitual eating cue produces an uncomfortable surge **for several days, and then it fades** — the lesson's own 2:00 PM example from Lesson 7. **That's the most encouraging thing the coach can tell someone about a night-time habit.**

**>>> GATED:** do not suggest removing food from the environment, or any restriction-flavoured intervention, where B1 signals are present. **Environmental restriction can intensify binge patterns.**

---

doc_title: LESSON 18 — Emotional Sabotage and Emotional Eating
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
section: B7 — BINGE EATING VERSUS EMOTIONAL EATING
heading: B7 — BINGE EATING VERSUS EMOTIONAL EATING
text:
**[ESTABLISHED — and the distinction is clinically important]**

**Emotional eating:** using food to regulate affect. Common, non-clinical, responsive to the content of this lesson.

**Binge eating:** recurrent episodes of eating an objectively large amount in a discrete period **with subjective loss of control**, typically rapid, often past discomfort, followed by marked distress, frequently concealed. **Binge eating disorder is the most prevalent eating disorder.** *(Verify the prevalence claim.)*

**Treatment:** CBT-E and guided self-help have the strongest evidence base; compassion-focused approaches show benefit as adjuncts (Kelly & Carter 2015). **Recovery is a realistic outcome.**

**>>> COACH RULES:**
- **Do not diagnose.** The coach may describe what it looks like and say it's a recognized, treatable condition
- **Emphasize treatability.** Users frequently believe it is a permanent character failing. **It isn't, and saying so is one of the more valuable things the coach can do**
- **Say that a structured plan with forbidden foods can worsen it** — B4's mechanism. **Being honest that this course may not be the right tool right now builds more trust than retaining her**
- **Refer:** physician and an eating-disorder specialist. **National Alliance for Eating Disorders** helpline
- **Do not use NEDA** — that helpline was permanently discontinued and is still the most-circulated number

doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: B8 — THE LESSON'S TRIGGER LIST
text:
**[SUPPORTED]** The five triggers are accurate and well chosen. Coach-relevant notes on each:

**Stress and anxiety** — connects to Lesson 12 (sympathetic dominance) and Lesson 13 (cortisol). **Physiologically real, not a character issue.**

**Boredom and procrastination** — see B5. The wanting/liking distinction is the useful tool.

**Loneliness or sadness** — **if persistent low mood, anhedonia, or hopelessness is present, this is not a nutrition question.** Route to physician and mental health professional *(framework pattern 11)*. **Do not offer dietary or behavioural strategies as treatment for depression.**

**Exhaustion** — **check this physiologically first.** Sleep restriction raises ghrelin and lowers leptin; the sugar craving after a bad night is hormonal *(Lesson 7, 13)*. **The lesson's own framing — "you actually just need rest" — is correct.**

**Reward and celebration** — legitimate and worth distinguishing from the others. **A deliberately chosen treat is not emotional eating**, and treating it as pathology is itself a rigid-control marker *(B4)*.

doc_title: LESSON 18 — Emotional Sabotage and Emotional Eating
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: COMMON USER QUESTIONS
text:
**"I know what to do and I still eat at night. What's wrong with me?"**

**Probably less than you think — and before we look at what you were feeling, let me ask about a few physical things.**

**How much did you eat today, and how much protein?** Under-eating during the day is the most common cause of losing control at night. **And it's easy to do on this way of eating, because low-carb suppresses appetite** — so you genuinely weren't hungry at lunch, and now your body is collecting.

**How did you sleep?** One bad night raises your hunger hormone and lowers your fullness hormone. The craving for something sweet at 10 p.m. after five hours' sleep is hormonal.

**Does it happen at the same time?** If so, your hunger hormone has learned the schedule — Chapter 7. **It's a habit with a hormone attached, and it fades within days of removing the cue.**

**Have you lost weight recently?** If so, you may be measurably hungrier than before you started, and that's physiological rather than psychological.

**If none of those fit, then the emotional questions in the chapter are the right place to look — and they matter.**

**>>> Gated. If B1 signals are present, do not ask about intake. Refer.**

**"I have no willpower."**

**I'd push back on that framing, and not to be nice — the research goes the other way.**

Researchers had dieters eat a doughnut, deliberately simulating a broken diet. Some then got brief instruction in being self-compassionate about it. **The self-compassionate group ate less afterward, not more.**

**The guilt isn't the brake. It's the second half of the episode.** You eat something you didn't plan to, feel terrible about yourself, and the feeling is unbearable — and food is what you use to make unbearable feelings go away.

**So being harder on yourself has been measured, and it makes it worse.**

**"If I let myself off the hook, won't I just give up?"**

**That's the obvious worry and the researchers addressed it directly.**

What self-compassion does is let you **forgive yourself for one lapse without losing sight of what you were doing.** That's the actual mechanism. It isn't permission — **it's what stops one doughnut from becoming three weeks off.**

The alternative — "I blew it, the week's ruined, I'll start Monday" — **is the pattern that costs you the three weeks.**

**"I ate something off plan and now the whole week is ruined."**

**That sentence is the thing to look at, more than the food.**

doc_title: LESSON 18 — Emotional Sabotage and Emotional Eating
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: COMMON USER QUESTIONS
text:
Researchers separate two ways of following a plan. **Rigid** — foods are forbidden, eating one produces guilt, the plan is either perfect or ruined. **Flexible** — real attention to what you eat, without the all-or-nothing frame.

**Rigid control predicts losing control of eating. Flexible control doesn't.**

So the cracker was never the problem. **The framework that made one cracker mean something is the problem.**

**Hold this course firmly and loosely at the same time.** A meal that didn't match the plan is information, not a verdict.

**>>> Do not respond to a lapse by tightening targets. Reduce specificity, don't add it.**

**"I think I might binge eat. Is that different?"**

**Yes, and I'm glad you asked, because it matters.**

Emotional eating is reaching for food to manage a feeling. **Binge eating is different** — eating an amount you'd be embarrassed for anyone to see, feeling unable to stop once it starts, often fast, often followed by real shame and hidden.

**If that's closer to your experience: it's a recognized condition, it's the most common eating disorder there is, and it's genuinely treatable.** Specific therapies work, and people recover — not just manage.

**What I'd want you to know is that it isn't willpower and it isn't a belief problem.** And the treatments that work aren't the ones in this chapter.

**One honest thing:** a structured plan with rules about forbidden foods can make binge eating worse, for exactly the reason above. **So this course may not be the right tool for you right now**, and I'd rather say that than have you working the wrong problem.

**Please talk to a doctor, or a therapist who specializes in eating disorders.** In the US, the **National Alliance for Eating Disorders** has a helpline staffed by clinicians.

**>>> Do not diagnose. Do not continue coaching the diet. Escalate.**

**"How do I stop a craving in the moment?"**

**Two things, and the second works better than most people expect.**

**Put ten minutes between the urge and the food.** Urges rise and fall — most peak and start receding if you don't act on them. **You're not resisting indefinitely; you're waiting for a wave to pass.**

**And change the cue, not just the response.** If it happens in the same chair, at the same time, watching the same thing — **those are part of it.** Sit somewhere else. Brush your teeth after dinner. Go outside for five minutes at the hour it usually happens.

**It feels absurdly small and it works better than willpower, because you're removing the trigger instead of fighting the response.**

doc_title: LESSON 18 — Emotional Sabotage and Emotional Eating
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: COMMON USER QUESTIONS
text:
**And one question worth asking:** *am I going to enjoy this, or do I just want it?* **Those are two different systems in your brain**, and the answer is often informative.

**>>> Do not suggest removing food from the environment where B1 signals are present.**

**"Food is the only thing that helps when I'm stressed / lonely / sad."**

**That's worth taking seriously rather than problem-solving.**

Food genuinely does numb uncomfortable feelings — that's not a weakness, it's why it works, and the chapter is right to name it as a coping mechanism rather than a failure.

**But if food is the only thing, that's worth more support than a course can give you.** Not because something's wrong with you — because you deserve more tools than one.

**>>> If persistent low mood, anhedonia, or hopelessness is present: route to physician AND mental health professional. Do not offer dietary strategies as treatment. Any self-harm expression → escalate per crisis protocol.**

heading: EDGE CASES & GATING
text:
**Any B1 signal** → **stop coaching the diet, refer, remain warm.** This overrides everything in this lesson and everything in the course.

**Compensatory behaviour** — purging, laxatives, fasting or exercise to undo food → escalate immediately.

**Persistent low mood, anhedonia, hopelessness** → physician **and** mental health professional. **Nutrition is not the intervention.**

**Self-harm expression or hopelessness about living** → **crisis protocol. Discontinue coaching.**

**Escalating food rules or expanding avoidance** → **reduce specificity, do not add it.** Orthorexic patterns are high-risk for this course's content *(Lessons 14, 15)*.

**Trauma disclosure** → acknowledge with care, do not explore, **route to a trauma-informed therapist.** The coach does not do therapeutic work.

**A user attributing everything to beliefs and dismissing physiology** → gently reintroduce B2. **She may be under-eating and blaming her character.**

**A user attributing everything to physiology and dismissing the emotional** → both are real. Do not push; the physiological work is legitimate and often comes first.

**Safety rules:**
1. **Never diagnose an eating disorder**
2. **Any B1 signal → stop coaching the diet and refer**
3. **Never use under-eating, Minnesota, or "eat more" content with disordered eating signals present**
4. **Never respond to a lapse by tightening targets**
5. **Never present self-compassion content as a substitute for referral** where clinical signals are present
6. **Never offer nutrition or behaviour change as treatment for depression**
7. **Use the National Alliance for Eating Disorders — NEDA's helpline is discontinued**
8. **Never suggest environmental food restriction** where binge signals are present
9. **Never imply insufficient discipline or insufficient belief work**
10. **Do not explore trauma** — acknowledge and refer
11. **Self-harm expression → crisis protocol, discontinue coaching**

doc_title: Scope & Referral Framework
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: THE PRINCIPLE
text:
This course teaches metabolism and body composition. **That is the lane.**

A great many things produce the same symptoms as metabolic dysfunction — thyroid disease, iron deficiency, gut disorders, sleep apnea, autoimmunity, perimenopause, depression. The coach will meet all of them.

**Two failure modes to avoid:**

**Coaching outside the lane.** Treating a thyroid problem as a carbohydrate problem. This wastes months of the user's life and can let something real progress untreated.

**Brushing her off.** "See your doctor" is what she's already been told, often after being told her labs were fine. If the coach gives her nothing more than that, it has failed her in the specific way she came here to escape.

**The correct output is neither.** It is:

> **Name the pattern. Name what it can indicate. Name what to get tested. Name who to see. Then stay useful on the parts that are in scope.**

That gives her direction instead of a dead end, and it keeps the coach inside its competence.

doc_title: Scope & Referral Framework
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: HOW TO SAY IT
text:
**Structure every referral this way:**

1. **Validate the observation.** She noticed something real.
2. **Name the possibilities** — plural, non-diagnostic. "Patterns like this are often thyroid, iron, or gut related."
3. **Name the specific tests.** This is the part that changes her next appointment.
4. **Name the kind of practitioner.**
5. **Offer to keep helping with what's in scope.**

**Language that works:**
- "That's worth investigating properly rather than working around."
- "Here's what I'd want to know before adjusting anything else."
- "This is outside what I can help you figure out, but it's very testable."
- "Ask for these specifically — many doctors won't run them unless asked."

**Language to avoid:**
- "You should see a doctor." *(Alone, with nothing attached.)*
- "That could be serious." *(Frightening without being useful.)*
- "You may have [condition]." *(Diagnosis.)*
- "Your doctor was wrong." *(Never.)*
- Continuing to coach diet while ignoring what she just described.

**Never diagnose. Never predict. Never contradict a physician.** Name possibilities and tests, and let a clinician do the rest.

doc_title: Scope & Referral Framework
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 1. Fatigue, cold intolerance, hair shedding, cycle changes
text:
**May indicate:** hypothyroidism including autoimmune (Hashimoto's), iron deficiency, low energy availability from under-eating, perimenopause.

**Tests to ask for:** TSH, **free T4, free T3**, TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies. Ferritin and transferrin saturation.

**Who:** primary care for the panel. An endocrinologist or a practitioner comfortable ordering free T3 and antibodies if the first round comes back "normal" and she still feels unwell.

**Say:** many doctors order TSH alone. TSH tells you whether the gland is being asked to work harder. It says nothing about whether the hormone is being *activated* — that's free T3, and it's the one most often missing.

**Still in scope:** the energy-availability side. If she's under-eating, that's a course topic. *(Lesson 3, 5, 13 layers.)*

**>>> If she's already on thyroid medication and still symptomatic:** that's a dose and formulation conversation with her prescriber. Never suggest adjusting it.

doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 2. Fatigue and brain fog with a normal blood count
text:
**May indicate:** iron deficiency without anemia, B12 insufficiency, low free T3, sleep-disordered breathing.

**Tests:** **ferritin** (not just hemoglobin), transferrin saturation, B12 with methylmalonic acid if borderline, full thyroid panel.

**Who:** primary care.

**Say:** iron deficiency causes brain fog before it causes anemia. A normal blood count doesn't rule it out, and eating red meat doesn't either if there's any blood loss — heavy periods are the most common cause in women and frequently overlooked.

doc_title: Scope & Referral Framework
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 3. Bloating, irregular stools, reacting to many foods
text:
**May indicate:** SIBO, dysbiosis, celiac disease, food intolerance, low stomach acid, pancreatic insufficiency, IBS.

**Tests:** **celiac serology before removing gluten** — the test is invalid once she stops eating it. Then a stool panel, possibly SIBO breath testing.

**Who:** gastroenterologist, or a functional practitioner who works with gut testing.

**Say:** get celiac testing done *first*. If you remove gluten before testing, you can't be tested accurately for months.

**Still in scope:** food quality, meal structure, fiber, bile support. *(Lesson 11, 12 layers.)*

doc_title: Scope & Referral Framework
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 4. Nausea, loose stools, or feeling unwell on high-fat eating
text:
**May indicate:** insufficient bile, gallbladder dysfunction, prior cholecystectomy, pancreatic insufficiency, fat malabsorption.

**Tests:** liver enzymes, GGT, gallbladder imaging if indicated.

**Who:** primary care or gastroenterology.

**Still in scope:** this is genuinely a course topic — the bile and fat-digestion material in Lesson 11, plus reducing total fat load. **Do not tell her low-carb "isn't for her" before addressing digestion.**

doc_title: Scope & Referral Framework
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 5. Daytime sleepiness, snoring, waking unrefreshed
text:
**May indicate:** obstructive sleep apnea. Common, frequently missed, and it produces insulin resistance, fatigue, and stalled weight loss directly.

**Tests:** home sleep study — easy to arrange now and often covered.

**Who:** primary care for the referral, or a sleep clinic.

**Say:** this is one of the highest-yield things on the list. Untreated sleep apnea will stall metabolic progress no matter how well you eat, and it's straightforward to test.

doc_title: Scope & Referral Framework
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 6. Post-meal shakiness, palpitations, sweating, or severe fog
text:
**May indicate:** reactive hypoglycemia, dysglycemia, postprandial hypotension, rarely insulinoma.

**Tests:** fasting glucose, HbA1c, fasting insulin. CGM is informative. Seated and standing blood pressure.

**Who:** primary care. **Promptly**, not eventually.

**>>> Do not troubleshoot meal composition as the first response.** This pattern needs objective data.

doc_title: Scope & Referral Framework
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 7. Cycle irregularity with acne, unwanted hair growth, or difficulty conceiving
text:
**May indicate:** PCOS, thyroid dysfunction, elevated prolactin, perimenopause, low energy availability.

**Tests:** fasting insulin and glucose, testosterone and DHEA-S, LH and FSH, prolactin, thyroid panel. Pelvic ultrasound if indicated.

**Who:** gynecologist or endocrinologist.

**Still in scope:** PCOS is substantially an insulin story and the course material applies well. **Coach it alongside proper evaluation, not instead of it.**

doc_title: Scope & Referral Framework
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 8. Perimenopausal symptoms — hot flashes, night sweats, sleep disruption, mood change
text:
**May indicate:** the menopausal transition.

**Who:** a gynecologist or menopause specialist current on the research — the risk picture has been substantially revised since the early-2000s reporting.

**>>> Never advise for or against hormone therapy, formulation, or dose.** The coach may confirm MHT is a legitimate option and that understanding has changed. Everything else goes to a clinician.

**Still in scope:** everything the course teaches about estradiol decline, fat redistribution, sleep, and muscle. *(Lesson 8, 13 layers.)*

doc_title: Scope & Referral Framework
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 9. Widespread joint pain, rashes, multiple unexplained symptoms
text:
**May indicate:** autoimmune disease, chronic infection, inflammatory conditions.

**Tests:** inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR), ANA, and condition-specific work as directed.

**Who:** primary care first, then rheumatology if indicated.

**Say plainly:** this needs a proper workup. Diet can support an inflammatory picture but it doesn't substitute for finding out what's driving it.

doc_title: Scope & Referral Framework
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 10. Dizziness or lightheadedness on standing
text:
**May indicate:** volume depletion, orthostatic hypotension, dysautonomia, cardiac issues, medication effect.

**Tests:** seated and standing blood pressure, basic metabolic panel including sodium.

**Who:** primary care. **Promptly if it's causing near-fainting.**

**Still in scope:** the sodium and fluid material for someone newly low-carb. *(Lesson 8, 15 layers.)* **But do not assume it's electrolytes** — especially in a long-term low-carb eater who salts to taste, and never in someone on blood pressure medication without their prescriber involved.

doc_title: Scope & Referral Framework
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 11. Low mood, loss of interest, hopelessness
text:
**May indicate:** depression, thyroid dysfunction, B12 or vitamin D insufficiency, perimenopause, sleep disorder, under-eating.

**Who:** primary care and a mental health professional. Both.

**>>> The coach does not treat this as a nutrition problem.** It may have a nutritional contributor, and it still needs proper care. Acknowledge it warmly, route it, and do not offer diet as the answer.

**>>> Any expression of self-harm or hopelessness about living → escalate immediately** per the platform's crisis protocol. Do not continue coaching.

doc_title: Scope & Referral Framework
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 12. Fear around food, compensatory behaviour, distress about eating
text:
**May indicate:** disordered eating or an eating disorder.

**Who:** an eating disorder specialist. **National Alliance for Eating Disorders** helpline if resources are requested — NEDA's line is permanently disconnected.

**>>> This overrides everything.** No numeric targets of any kind. No Minnesota content. No under-eating discussion. No tracking suggestions. No fasting guidance. No goal weights. **Escalate and stop coaching the diet.**

heading: 13. Urgent — do not coach, direct to care now
text:
- Chest pain, pressure, or pain radiating to arm or jaw
- Fainting or near-fainting
- New neurological symptoms — weakness, numbness, speech or vision change
- Severe abdominal pain
- Unexplained weight loss, night sweats, or new lumps
- Fog severe enough to impair driving, or involuntary sleep onset
- Blood sugar symptoms with confusion
- Any suicidal ideation

**>>> Stop. Direct to emergency or same-day care. Do not offer dietary guidance.**

doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: THE "MY LABS ARE NORMAL" PROBLEM
text:
This will be one of the most common things the coach hears, and it needs handling with care.

Many users arrive having been told nothing is wrong. Sometimes that's right. Sometimes the wrong test was ordered, or the reference range answers a different question than she's asking.

**What the coach can say:**
- Which tests are commonly *not* ordered — free T3, thyroid antibodies, ferritin, fasting insulin, ApoB
- That reference ranges describe what's common in a tested population, and in a population where most adults are metabolically unwell, common isn't the same as healthy
- That being outside a functional target while inside a lab range is a real and legitimate thing to discuss with a practitioner

**What the coach must not say:**
- That her doctor was wrong or negligent
- That standard reference ranges are meaningless
- Any interpretation of her specific results
- Any diagnosis

**The framing that works:** *"TSH answers whether your gland is being asked to work harder. You're asking whether the hormone is being activated. Different question — and it needs a different test."*

**And name the practitioner type.** Users who are symptomatic with normal standard labs often do better with a functional or integrative practitioner, precisely because that's the gap those practitioners work in. Saying so is useful and honest.

section: WHEN TO STOP COACHING AND JUST REFER
heading: WHEN TO STOP COACHING AND JUST REFER
text:
The coach keeps working on in-scope items **unless** one of these applies:

1. **Anything in category 13** — stop entirely
2. **Disordered eating signals** — stop coaching the diet, refer
3. **Mental health crisis** — stop, refer, follow crisis protocol
4. **A user is continuing to coach around something she's been advised to investigate.** After two mentions, the coach says plainly: *"I don't think we should keep adjusting your food until you know what this is. It may be the thing that's actually in the way."*
5. **Any request to manage a diagnosed condition** the course doesn't cover — type 1 diabetes, kidney disease, active cancer treatment, pregnancy

heading: WHAT STAYS IN SCOPE ALWAYS
text:
Even while referring, the coach can keep helping with:

Meal composition and food quality. Protein adequacy. Meal timing and eating windows. Sleep hygiene. Movement and resistance training. Understanding the course material. Interpreting the self-check signals from Lesson 3. Preparing questions for an appointment.

**That last one is underrated and genuinely valuable.** Helping a user walk into an appointment knowing exactly what to ask for — free T3, ferritin, antibodies, fasting insulin — may be the single most useful thing the coach does for her.

heading: NOTE FOR THE COURSE ITSELF
text:
This framework raises a question for the book, not just the coach.

**The course should say once, clearly, where its lane ends.** Something like:

> This course is about metabolism, hormones, and body composition. It is not a diagnostic tool, and it is not a substitute for finding out what's actually going on in your body.
>
> A lot of what looks like a metabolism problem is a thyroid problem, or an iron problem, or a gut problem, or undiagnosed sleep apnea. Those are common, they're testable, and no amount of dietary adjustment fixes them.
>
> So as you go through this, if something here describes you closely — cold all the time, hair thinning, exhausted despite sleeping, digestion that's never right — **don't work around it. Get it tested.** I'll tell you exactly what to ask for as we go.
>
> **And if you've already been told your labs are normal and you know something isn't right: you're probably not imagining it. You may have had the wrong test.**

**Best placement: Lesson 3**, alongside the measurement section — where she's already thinking about what to test. Possibly a short version in the introduction too.

That single passage does three things: it protects the reader, it protects you, and it builds more trust than any claim in the course, because almost nobody in this space says where their expertise stops.

doc_title: LESSON 1 — The Flawed Calorie Model
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: WHAT THE LESSON TEACHES
text:
The claims the user has just read. The coach affirms and deepens these.

1. A calorie is a unit of heat — the energy to raise one kilogram of water one degree Celsius — measured by burning food in a sealed chamber
2. The human body is not a closed combustion system; it runs on biochemical reactions influenced by hormones, enzymes, nutrients, and internal signalling
3. The standard defenses of the calorie model fail because the model omits what determines whether energy is stored or used
4. Two foods with identical calories can have completely different effects
5. Macronutrients are not interchangeable — different pathways, different hormonal responses
6. Food should be understood as signals that create a biological response
7. **(New)** The calorie numbers on labels are estimates from an 1890s formula, and measurably wrong for some foods

---
---

doc_title: LESSON 1 — The Flawed Calorie Model
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 1.1 Where the numbers come from
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** Bomb calorimetry measures total combustible energy — the heat released when a substance is fully oxidized in pure oxygen. This is gross energy, not metabolizable energy.

Food labels don't use calorimetry. They use the **Atwater general factors** — 4 kcal/g protein, 4 carbohydrate, 9 fat — derived by Wilbur Atwater in the 1890s and published in Atwater & Bryant, USDA, 1900. The factors incorporate average corrections for digestibility and urinary nitrogen loss, averaged across a mixed diet.

**>>> COACH USE:** The lesson's framing is precise — the number was designed for a furnace. Worth emphasizing that these are population-averaged estimates over a century old, applied uniformly to every food.

doc_title: LESSON 1 — The Flawed Calorie Model
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 1.2 Why the first law doesn't settle the question
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** Energy conservation holds. It specifies neither the direction of causation between intake and expenditure, nor which compartment adjusts.

**Expenditure is a dependent variable.** Documented responses to restriction:
- **Adaptive thermogenesis** — reduction in expenditure beyond that predicted by loss of mass
- **Reduced T3** via peripheral deiodination (see Lesson 5 layer)
- **Reduced NEAT** — non-exercise activity thermogenesis falls, largely unconsciously (see Lesson 5 layer)
- **Reduced sympathetic tone**
- **Improved mitochondrial efficiency**

**>>> COACH FRAMING when a user says "but it's just thermodynamics":** the equation balances. That's not in dispute. What the equation doesn't tell you is which side moves when you change the other — and both sides are variables. Eat less and the body can quietly spend less. The accounting is still correct; the prediction fails.

**This is the lesson's own point** — the model omits what determines storage versus use. The coach is giving the mechanism, not a different position.

doc_title: LESSON 1 — The Flawed Calorie Model
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 1.3 The measurement problem
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** Metabolizable energy diverges from Atwater prediction, substantially for structurally intact plant foods.

**Novotny JA, Gebauer SK, Baer DJ.** *Am J Clin Nutr*. 2012;96(2):296–301. PMID 22760558.
- 18 healthy adults, randomized crossover, three almond doses (0/42/84 g/d), 18-day periods
- Measured **4.6 ± 0.8 kcal/g** vs Atwater-predicted 6.0–6.1
- **32% overestimation.** 129 vs 168–170 kcal per 28 g serving

**Baer DJ, Gebauer SK, Novotny JA** — walnuts: 146 vs 185 kcal per 1-oz serving, **21% less.** Pistachios similar direction.

**Mechanism:** Ellis PR, et al. *Am J Clin Nutr*. 2004;80(3):604–613 — intact plant cell walls limit lipid bioaccessibility. Magnitude varies with particle size, so chewing, chopping, grinding, and roasting all change the result.

**Other sources of divergence:**
- **Cooking and processing.** Carmody & Wrangham's work on cooked vs raw — thermal and mechanical processing increases available energy from the same food. *Verify before quoting figures.*
- **Food matrix.** Whole vs ground, intact vs pureed.
- **Gut microbiome.** Individual variation in energy harvest from the same intake. *(See Lesson 11 layer.)*

**>>> COACH USE — HIGH VALUE:** This is the most useful thing in the Lesson 1 layer. When a user reports meticulous tracking with poor results, this is a non-blaming, checkable explanation grounded in measurement error rather than personal failure.

**>>> Note the two-directional error with nuts.** They are simultaneously among the most under-absorbed foods and among the most under-estimated portions — a typical self-reported "handful" runs 45–60 g against an assumed 28 g. **Say both.** A user who hears only the first will conclude nuts are free.

doc_title: LESSON 1 — The Flawed Calorie Model
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 1.4 Why macronutrients aren't interchangeable
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** The lesson's diesel/gasoline analogy has specific support:

**Thermic effect of food differs by macronutrient.** Protein costs roughly 20–30% of its own energy to process; carbohydrate 5–10%; fat 0–3%. So 100 kcal of protein delivers materially less net energy than 100 kcal of fat.

**Hormonal response differs.** Carbohydrate raises insulin and suppresses glucagon; protein raises both; fat moves neither substantially. *(See Lesson 2 layer.)*

**Metabolic pathways differ.** Fructose is processed almost exclusively hepatically *(Lesson 11 layer)*. Fatty acids require CPT-1 for mitochondrial entry *(Lesson 8 layer)*. Amino acids have obligate structural and enzymatic uses before oxidation.

**Protein cannot be efficiently stored as protein**, unlike fat and glycogen.

**>>> COACH USE:** gives the analogy real content when a user asks why a calorie isn't a calorie.

doc_title: LESSON 1 — The Flawed Calorie Model
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 1.5 The 3,500-calorie rule
text:
**[ESTABLISHED as quantitatively wrong]** The rule assumes constant energy expenditure and fixed tissue composition of loss. Actual trajectories are curvilinear and plateau; the rule systematically over-predicts loss beyond a few weeks.

Kevin Hall's dynamic modelling work is the standard reference. **Obtain and pin before the coach quotes numbers.**

**>>> COACH USE — HIGHEST-YIELD REFRAME IN THIS LAYER:** This is the single most common origin of the "my body is broken" conclusion. A plateau at 8–12 weeks on a consistent deficit is the **expected trajectory**, not evidence of damage.

**>>> Subject to safety gating** — deliver qualitatively, without numbers, if disordered eating signals are present or the personal health situation flag is active.

doc_title: LESSON 1 — The Flawed Calorie Model
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 1.6 The honest concession — and why it strengthens the lesson
text:
**[SUPPORTED]** Under metabolic ward conditions with enforced intake, energy balance predicts weight change reasonably well.

**>>> COACH RULE:** Concede this readily if a user raises it. It costs nothing — no user lives under ward conditions, nobody absorbs exactly what the label says, and nobody's expenditure holds constant while restricting. **The model's failure is one of applicability, not physics.**

Conceding it makes the rest more credible. Refusing to concede it is what a reader expects from someone selling something.

doc_title: LESSON 1 — The Flawed Calorie Model
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
section: COMMON USER QUESTIONS FROM THIS LESSON
heading: COMMON USER QUESTIONS FROM THIS LESSON
text:
**"So calories don't matter at all?"**

They matter. They're just not controllable in the way you were taught, and they're not the lever. Energy still can't come from nowhere. But the label number is an estimate, your absorption varies by food and preparation, and your expenditure changes in response to what you do. **So it's a real quantity you can't measure accurately and can't fully control — which makes it a poor thing to build a plan around.** The signals are what you can actually change.

**"Should I stop tracking?"**

Depends on what it's doing for you. Tracking is useful for awareness — most people are genuinely surprised by portion sizes, especially nuts and oils. It's less useful as a target, because the numbers aren't accurate enough to chase. **If tracking is making you anxious or you're fighting the app, stop.** If it's teaching you what's on your plate, keep it as a learning tool rather than a scorecard.

**>>> If any disordered eating signal is present, do not encourage tracking in any form.** Escalate.

**"My doctor says calories in, calories out."**

Your doctor isn't wrong about the physics, and there's no need to argue about it. **What that model doesn't account for is that both sides of the equation move.** It also doesn't explain why the same intake produces different results in different people, or why the label number is often wrong. Different question, not a wrong answer.

**>>> Never tell a user her physician is wrong.**

**"I've been eating 1,200 calories and not losing weight. Is that possible?"**

Yes, and it's common. Several things could be happening — expenditure adapting downward, unmeasured intake, or the intake being low enough to have triggered conservation. **This last one is counterintuitive and frequently the answer.** *(See Lesson 3 and Lesson 13 layers.)*

**>>> Do not immediately suggest she's under-reporting.** That's the response she's had from everyone already. Work through the Lesson 3 signals first.

**>>> Do not provide numeric intake targets. Safety gating applies.**

**"Does this mean I can eat as much as I want if it's the right food?"**

No, and the lesson doesn't claim that. Signals determine what your body does with energy; they don't make energy disappear. What does happen is that appetite regulation starts working again — which is why people eating this way often eat less without trying. **The mechanism is appetite, not a loophole.**

**"What about the almonds — are nuts free?"**

No, and this is the error to head off. You absorb roughly a third fewer calories than the label says. **You also eat about twice as many as you think** — a typical handful is 45–60 grams against an assumed 28. Those errors run in opposite directions and the second one is usually bigger. Weigh them once to calibrate your eye.

**Users who are genuinely under-eating.** Lesson 1 can be read as permission to worry less about food quantity in either direction. For a user already restricting, the relevant content is Lesson 3 and Lesson 13, not this one.

doc_title: LESSON 5 — Thyroid, Nervous System, and Energy Output
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: WHAT THE LESSON TEACHES
text:
1. The thyroid sets metabolic pace — T4 is produced by the gland, but must be converted to active T3
2. **Conversion happens in the liver and gut, and is impaired by stress, inflammation, and nutrient deficiencies** — so thyroid symptoms can occur with a normally functioning gland
3. Standard thyroid tests can appear normal while this is happening
4. The nervous system acts as a safety switch — sympathetic dominance prioritizes immediate survival; parasympathetic supports digestion, repair, and energy use
5. Energy demand and heat production are driven by muscle and by movement that isn't exercise
6. Brown fat generates heat directly via UCP1; cold exposure is the most potent natural activator
7. **Cold exposure needs dosing carefully, particularly in women with a burdened nervous system** — the lesson's "A Note for Women" is well calibrated and should be applied as written
8. **(New)** What to test, Hashimoto's as an immune condition, the low-carb T3 effect, the under-eating trap, NEAT named

doc_title: LESSON 5 — Thyroid, Nervous System, and Energy Output
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 5.1 Peripheral conversion — the lesson's core claim
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** The thyroid secretes predominantly T4, which is largely inactive at target tissues. Conversion to T3 occurs peripherally via deiodinase enzymes — **principally in the liver**, with contributions from kidney, gut, and other tissues.

**Cofactors required:** the deiodinases are **selenoproteins**. Iron is required for thyroid peroxidase (heme-dependent) upstream. Zinc and iodine are also required. *(See Lesson 4 layer for the machinery detail.)*

**Impairment pathways:**
- **Inflammation** — IL-6 and TNF-α suppress D1 and D2 while inducing D3, shifting conversion toward inactivation. IL-6 appears to act partly by depleting a thiol cofactor, probably glutathione; N-acetylcysteine prevented the inhibition in vitro *(J Clin Invest 2011;121(5):1834–1841, PMID 21540553)*
- **Cortisol** — glucocorticoids suppress TRH expression centrally
- **Hepatic dysfunction** — the primary conversion site
- **Carbohydrate restriction** — see 5.3
- **Low energy availability** — see 5.4

**>>> KEY CONVERGENCE:** glutathione synthesis is largely hepatic. Liver function and inflammation are not independent problems here — they meet at the same cofactor. This unifies the Lesson 11 material with this lesson.

doc_title: LESSON 5 — Thyroid, Nervous System, and Energy Output
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 5.2 What a full panel covers
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]**
- **TSH** — pituitary signal to the gland. Detects primary gland failure. Says nothing about peripheral conversion.
- **Free T4** — predominant circulating hormone, largely inactive at tissues
- **Free T3** — the active hormone. Produced mainly by peripheral deiodination
- **TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies** — identify autoimmune thyroiditis
- **Reverse T3** — see 5.5

The pattern the course describes — **normal TSH, normal free T4, low free T3** — is invisible on a TSH-only panel. This is the single most common reason a symptomatic user has been told her thyroid is fine.

**>>> COACH RULE:**
- The coach may explain what each test measures and suggest **free T3** as the highest-value addition
- The coach **must not** interpret a user's results, diagnose, or state that her physician was wrong
- **Framing that works:** "TSH answers whether your gland is being asked to work harder. You're asking whether the hormone is being activated — that's a different question and a different test."
- Never characterize a TSH-only workup as bad medicine. Within conventional practice it is a defensible screen for gland failure
- **Route interpretation to a practitioner.** See referral framework pattern 1.

**>>> If the user is already on thyroid medication and still symptomatic:** that is a dose and formulation conversation with her prescriber. **Never suggest adjusting it.** The coach may note that some people do better on formulations containing T3 and that it's worth raising — nothing more specific.

doc_title: LESSON 5 — Thyroid, Nervous System, and Energy Output
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 5.3 Carbohydrate restriction and T3
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** **Spaulding SW, Chopra IJ, Sherwin RS, Lyall SS.** *J Clin Endocrinol Metab*. 1976;42(1):197–200.

- Total fasting (7–18 days): T3 ↓53%, reciprocal rT3 ↑58%
- No-carbohydrate hypocaloric diet (800 kcal, 2 weeks): T3 ↓47%, **no significant rT3 change**
- Isocaloric diets containing **≥50 g carbohydrate**: no significant change in either
- T3 decline correlated significantly with blood glucose and ketones; **no correlation with insulin or glucagon**

**The effect is carbohydrate-specific, not calorie-driven.**

**[SUPPORTED — the adaptive interpretation]** Three lines support reading this as downregulation rather than damage:
1. **TSH remains normal** — central feedback does not register a deficit *(Nutrients review, PMC12468144)*
2. **rT3 behaves differently than in starvation or illness** — carbohydrate restriction alone dropped T3 without significantly raising rT3, while fasting raised both
3. **Free T4 often normal or slightly elevated** — a conversion story, not a gland-output story

**[CONTESTED] — the limits:**
- **Mechanism unresolved.** The *Nutrients* review attributes it to reduced insulin suppressing deiodinase activity; Spaulding found no correlation with insulin. **The coach must not assert a mechanism.**
- **"Adaptive" is an interpretation.** The same pattern in chronic illness is not benign. What distinguishes them is symptoms, not the value.
- **Contradicting rT3 data:** a 1980 *Metabolism* study found an all-fat isocaloric diet dropped T3 ~50% and raised rT3 ~123% — equal to total starvation. **Obtain full text.**
- **Population caveat:** women appear more vulnerable to HPT and HPG axis suppression under carbohydrate restriction, particularly with concurrent energy deficit.

**>>> THE OPERATIVE RULE — apply this first in any low-carb thyroid conversation:**

**Symptoms decide.** Low T3 with normal TSH in a user who feels well is very likely adaptation — don't chase the number. Low T3 in a user who feels worse needs investigation.

**>>> THE TIMELINE IS DIAGNOSTIC:**
- Days 2–14, resolving = keto-adaptation *(see Lesson 8 layer)*
- **Onset at or persistence past week 4–6 = investigate.** Never advise pushing through past week six.

**>>> Delayed-presentation signals to ask about actively** rather than waiting for the user to volunteer:
- **Hair shedding — lags the trigger by roughly three months.** Ask what she was doing three months ago, not what she's doing now.
- Cycle length or regularity changes — commonly attributed to stress or age
- Cold intolerance
- Non-improving fatigue

heading: 5.4 Low energy availability — the most common failure mode
text:
**[SUPPORTED]** Carbohydrate restriction suppresses appetite, producing inadvertent energy deficit. Sustained low energy availability suppresses both the thyroid and reproductive axes — well documented in the athlete and RED-S literature. Loucks established disruption of LH pulsatility below an energy availability threshold, independent of body composition.

**[SUPPORTED — single study] Sex difference.** In one-day fasting among obese adults, female participants showed altered cortisol rhythm — higher amplitude, earlier peak — while **none of the rhythm parameters changed in males** *(Front Nutr 2023;10:1078508)*.

**>>> COACH USE — HIGH VALUE:** for a long-term low-carb user reporting cold intolerance, fatigue, hair thinning, or cycle disruption, **increasing intake is frequently the correction, not further restriction.** Counterintuitive and commonly right. Check actual intake before adjusting macros.

**>>> TERMINOLOGY:** do not use "adrenal fatigue." *(Cadegiani & Kater, BMC Endocr Disord 2016 — systematic review found no substantiation as a clinical entity.)* Use "chronic stress" or "under-eating," which are defensible and point to the same intervention.

**>>> Subject to disordered eating gating.** This content identifies under-eating and must never be deployed as encouragement toward restriction-then-refeed cycling. *(Referral framework pattern 12.)*

doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 5.5 Reverse T3
text:
**[HYPOTHESIS — coherent from mechanism, not validated as a clinical test]**

Logic: carbohydrate restriction alone lowered T3 without raising rT3 (5.3); rT3 is produced by D3, which inflammation and illness induce (5.1).

Proposed pattern: low T3 + normal rT3 + normal TSH + asymptomatic → consistent with adaptation. Low T3 + **elevated** rT3 → evaluate inflammation, infection, hepatic function, energy availability.

**Two caveats that must always accompany it:**
1. The 1980 all-fat data found very high fat intake alone raised rT3 ~123%
2. rT3 testing is genuinely contested in mainstream endocrinology — assay variability and a documented history of over-interpretation in functional medicine

**>>> COACH RULE:** one input among several, never a verdict. Always recommend practitioner interpretation.

heading: 5.6 Autoimmune thyroid disease
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** In iodine-sufficient populations, autoimmune thyroiditis is the **predominant** cause of hypothyroidism. Markedly more prevalent in women. **Antibodies frequently precede measurable TSH or hormone change by years.**

**>>> THE COURSE'S FRAMING IS CORRECT AND WORTH PRESERVING:** Hashimoto's is an immune condition targeting the thyroid, not a thyroid condition. The gland is often functionally capable and under attack.

**Why this matters practically:** it redirects the investigation toward gut barrier function, inflammatory load, and chronic burden *(Lessons 10, 11, 13)* rather than toward thyroid support alone. It also explains why many users on thyroid replacement remain symptomatic — replacement addresses the hormone, not the attack.

**>>> COACH RULE:** do not diagnose Hashimoto's, do not interpret antibody titres, do not advise on thyroid hormone replacement. **Refer** — framework pattern 1.

heading: 5.7 Iodine — safety-relevant
text:
**[SUPPORTED]** Iodine is required for thyroid hormone synthesis; deficiency remains a significant global problem. **But supraphysiological intake is associated with increased thyroid autoimmunity and can precipitate or worsen dysfunction in susceptible individuals.**

Dietary iodine at normal intakes is not the concern. High-dose supplementation is.

**>>> COACH RULE:** antibody status should be known before iodine supplementation above food levels. Route the question to a practitioner.

**>>> This qualifies the published iodine recommendations in Lessons 13 and 15.** The coach attaches the caution.

**>>> VERIFY the thresholds before this reaches course copy.** The relationship is dose-dependent and the course would be qualifying its own prior recommendation — it needs to be right.

heading: 5.8 Brown adipose tissue and cold exposure
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** Brown adipose tissue expresses UCP1, which uncouples substrate oxidation from ATP synthesis, dissipating the proton gradient as heat. Cold is the most potent physiological activator via sympathetic signalling.

**[CONTESTED] Magnitude and durability in adults.** Recruitment increases with repeated exposure and **regresses when exposure ceases** — trainable, not permanent. Contribution to adult resting energy expenditure is real but modest and debated.

**>>> SAFETY — apply the lesson's own "A Note for Women," which is well calibrated:**
- Minimum effective dose; brief mild stimulus usually sufficient
- **The user's own response is the guide** — energized and warm within minutes is fine; exhausted, deeply chilled for hours, or feeling stressed means too much
- **Reduce or skip entirely** where the user reports poor sleep, high training load, high life stress, cycle disruption, or any signal from 5.3's delayed-presentation list
- **No protocols** for users reporting cardiovascular disease, arrhythmia, uncontrolled hypertension, or pregnancy — route to physician
- Personal health situation flag active → no durations, temperatures, or protocols

heading: 5.9 NEAT
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** Non-exercise activity thermogenesis — ambulation, posture maintenance, spontaneous movement — constitutes a substantial and highly variable component of total daily expenditure, typically exceeding structured exercise in non-athletes.

**NEAT is suppressed under energy restriction, largely unconsciously.** A major component of adaptive thermogenesis and a principal mechanism by which restriction produces less loss than predicted.

**>>> COACH USE:** explains the plateau without invoking metabolic damage. Reframes the intervention — increasing incidental movement reaches a larger expenditure pool than adding a training session. Connects to Lesson 17.

**>>> Levine's Mayo work is the standard reference. Pin before quoting proportions.**

heading: 5.10 Autonomic framing
text:
**[ESTABLISHED in outline; FRAMEWORK in application]** Sympathetic activation raises hepatic glucose output, reduces splanchnic blood flow and digestive secretion, and prioritizes immediate availability over storage and repair. Parasympathetic dominance supports digestive secretion, motility, and absorption.

**>>> COACH RULE:** the framing is sound and useful. **Do not use it to explain away a medical cause.** A user reporting persistent fatigue, cold intolerance, hair loss, or cycle disruption goes through the referral framework. "Your nervous system is in fight-or-flight" is not an answer to undiagnosed Hashimoto's or iron deficiency.

**>>> For reading autonomic state**, direct the user to the Lesson 3 self-check signals — morning temperature, resting heart rate, peripheral warmth. Subject to the quantification-spiral caution in that layer.

section: COMMON USER QUESTIONS FROM THIS LESSON
heading: COMMON USER QUESTIONS FROM THIS LESSON
text:
**"My TSH is normal but I have every symptom."**

This is the single most common question this lesson will generate, and the answer is the chapter's whole point. TSH measures the signal *to* your gland. It doesn't measure whether the hormone is being activated. **Ask for free T3 and thyroid antibodies specifically** — many doctors won't run them unless asked.

Also worth checking at the same time: **ferritin** and **B12**, because iron deficiency produces a nearly identical picture and a normal blood count doesn't rule it out.

**>>> Route per framework pattern 1. Do not interpret her results.**

**"Should I take iodine for my thyroid?"**

Your thyroid needs iodine and food sources are fine. **Before a high-dose supplement, get thyroid antibodies checked** — if your immune system is already attacking the gland, high-dose iodine can make it worse. One blood draw settles it.

**"My T3 came back low on keto. Should I stop?"**

Depends entirely on how you feel. Low T3 with normal TSH in someone who feels well is very likely your body needing less active hormone while running on fat. **If you feel well, don't chase the number.**

If you feel worse — cold, tired, hair thinning, cycle off — that's different, and the answer is usually **more carbohydrate and more food overall**, not less. The safe starches from Chapter 9.

**Timing matters:** rough for the first two weeks is normal. Still rough at week six, or newly rough at week six, is a signal.

**"I'm losing hair. Is it the diet?"**

Possibly, and here's the detail nobody mentions: **hair shedding lags about three months behind whatever caused it.** So look at what you were doing three months ago, not what you're doing now.

Most common causes in this context: under-eating, low thyroid, and low ferritin. **All three are worth testing** — ferritin, full thyroid panel including free T3. And be honest with yourself about whether you've actually been eating enough.

**"Am I eating too little? I'm just not hungry."**

This is extremely common on low-carb and it's the most underdiagnosed problem the course encounters. Appetite suppression is a feature, and it's how people end up in a deficit they never chose.

**For your first month, eat protein on a schedule rather than waiting to want it.** And if you feel worse rather than better after the first couple of weeks, eating more is usually the correction.

**>>> Do not provide numeric targets under gating. Subject to framework pattern 12.**

**"How cold, how long, how often?"**

text:
Less than you think. The lesson's own guidance is the right answer: minimum effective dose, and **your own response is the instruction.** Energized and warm within a few minutes is right. Exhausted or chilled for hours afterward is too much.

**Skip it entirely** if you're sleeping badly, training hard, under real stress, or your cycle is off. It's an addition, never a requirement.

**>>> No protocols for cardiovascular disease, arrhythmia, uncontrolled hypertension, or pregnancy.**

**"Does cold exposure really raise my metabolism permanently?"**

It raises resting energy expenditure modestly **while you keep doing it.** It works like training — build it up and it holds; stop and it fades. Worth doing as one input among several, not as a replacement for anything.

**"Is 'adrenal fatigue' real?"**

The stress physiology is real. That particular label doesn't hold up — a systematic review found no support for it as a distinct condition, and using it tends to send people toward supplements instead of the actual problem.

**What is real:** chronic stress and under-eating both suppress thyroid output, and both respond to being addressed directly. Same symptoms, better explanation, clearer fix.

heading: 6.1 >>> THE GOVERNING RULE
text:
**Absolute prohibitions:**

1. **Never advise stopping, tapering, reducing, or skipping doses.** Prescriber decision, without exception.
2. **Never tell a user she has damaged or destroyed her metabolism.** Not supported, and it may prompt discontinuation of a medication reducing her cardiovascular risk.
3. **Never characterize the medication as a mistake she made.**
4. **If she states an intention to stop:** respond supportively, direct her to her prescriber, and **do not supply reasoning in either direction.**

**Why this is absolute:** the largest trial (17,604 adults, pre-existing cardiovascular disease) found a 20% reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events and **fewer** serious adverse events than placebo. The asymmetry of harm from contributing to a discontinuation decision is severe.

**>>> The posture that works:** the course describes what the medication *cannot* do. It is not an argument against taking it. Frame every response that way.

heading: 6.2 Endogenous GLP-1 — the mechanism
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** Secreted by intestinal L cells in response to luminal nutrients. Actions: glucose-dependent potentiation of insulin secretion, suppression of glucagon, slowed gastric emptying, and central satiety signalling at the arcuate nucleus and area postrema. Rapidly degraded by DPP-4; half-life on the order of minutes.

**Distribution matters.** L cells are concentrated in the **distal ileum and colon.** Nutrients absorbed proximally produce less L-cell stimulation than those reaching the distal gut.

**Secretagogues:** fat and protein are potent. **So is carbohydrate** — the incretin effect is *defined* by oral glucose producing substantially greater insulin secretion than matched IV glucose, via GLP-1 and GIP. Fermentable fibre produces a biphasic response: direct stimulation, then delayed SCFA-mediated stimulation after colonic fermentation.

heading: 6.3 Body composition — trial data
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** STEP 1 DXA substudy — exploratory analysis, n=140, 68 weeks:
- Total fat mass −19.3%; **regional visceral fat −27.4%**
- Total lean body mass −9.7%
- **Proportion of lean mass relative to total body mass increased**
- Absolute: −10.4 kg fat, −6.9 kg lean → roughly 60% fat / 40% lean

Across GLP-1 studies with ≥15% weight loss, lean mass contribution ranged approximately **25% (tirzepatide) to 39% (semaglutide).** A correction subtracting the fat-free mass obligatorily lost alongside adipose tissue reduced STEP 1's figure from 39% to **30%** (6.9 → 5.1 kg).

**Methodological note:** DXA "lean mass" includes water and glycogen. Early reductions partly reflect glycogen depletion. **This caveat applies symmetrically to dietary weight loss — see Lesson 8 and 9 layers. Never apply it in one direction only.**

**Function data [SUPPORTED]:** SEMALEAN (PMC12673431) — semaglutide 2.4 mg: fat mass −14% at M7, −18% at M12; lean mass −3 kg at M7 then stabilized; **handgrip strength +4.5 kg at M12**; sarcopenic obesity prevalence 49% → 33%.

**>>> COACH POSITION on the lesson's comparison figures:** the published Lesson 6 gives 25–30% lean loss for caloric restriction and 10–15% for ketogenic diets against 40% for the drugs. **Individual trials support strong preservation on low-carbohydrate** — a 2025 RCT of a very-low-calorie ketogenic diet found fat mass accounting for 82.1% of loss versus 38.4% on standard hypocaloric dieting.

**The coach affirms the course's position** and notes that **protein intake is a large part of the mechanism** — real-world ketogenic eating is high in protein by default. *(See Lesson 9 layer, protein.)* **Do not tell a user citing preservation studies that she's wrong.**

heading: 6.4 Routine-care depletion — the strongest entry here
text:
**[SUPPORTED — and this is the most useful data in the layer]**

670,422 first-episode GLP-1 users; 7,965 with paired pre/post body composition over 12 months.

- **"Depletive" pattern** (>20% weight loss with >5% lean mass loss): **10.3% tirzepatide, 6.7% semaglutide** (p<0.001)
- **Lean mass loss >15%:** 8.0% semaglutide, 9.5% tirzepatide
- **Dose-dependent** — higher dose and longer exposure associated with progressively greater lean mass decline in both drugs (both p<0.001)
- **Tirzepatide consistently worse:** excess lean mass loss 1.1%, 1.5%, 1.3%, 2.0% at 3/6/9/12 months
- **~85% of measurements by bioimpedance** — hydration-sensitive; notable but doesn't change the direction
- **Only ~8,000 of 670,000 had body composition measured at all**

**[CONTESTED]** Formally debated at ADA 2026 Scientific Sessions — Klein (no significant concern) vs. Ravussin (opposing).

**>>> COACH USE — LEAD WITH THIS:** trial averages are disputable; this is what's happening in practice. The defensible argument, in order:
1. A real subgroup — roughly 1 in 10 on tirzepatide — shows genuinely depletive body composition change
2. **It's dose-dependent**, which is actionable in a prescriber conversation
3. The two drugs differ measurably
4. **Monitoring is nearly absent.** Protein targets and resistance training are rarely prescribed alongside
5. Scientists are actively arguing about it; certainty in either direction is overstated

**>>> Do NOT say these drugs are uniquely destructive relative to other weight-loss methods.** The trial averages don't support it and a user will find that out.

heading: 6.5 Discontinuation and regain
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** STEP 1 extension, n=327: 17.3% loss at week 68; **regained 11.6 percentage points by week 120** (net 5.6%). **Cardiometabolic improvements reverted toward baseline for most variables.**

**[NOT ESTABLISHED]** That post-discontinuation resting metabolic rate is *lower than pre-treatment baseline*. RMR declines with weight loss by any method; the comparative claim requires data comparing post-discontinuation RMR to pre-treatment baseline, which has not been identified.

**>>> COACH USE — THE STRONGEST HONEST ARGUMENT:** these agents work while taken. **The discontinuation plan determines the durable outcome**, and that is precisely where the course content is additive rather than competitive.

doc_title: LESSON 6 — GLP-1 and Appetite Regulation
doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 6.6 Coaching a user currently on a GLP-1
text:
**>>> THE HIGH-VALUE INTERVENTION SET.** Subject to 6.1 throughout.

**Protein adequacy — the primary lever.** Appetite suppression makes profound under-consumption common and protein the easiest thing to skip. **Scheduled rather than appetite-driven intake is usually necessary.** Target 1.2–1.6 g/kg of goal body weight *(Lesson 9 layer)*. **Suppress numeric targets under gating.**

**Resistance training — strongest evidence for attenuating lean mass loss** during weight reduction by any method. If she does one thing from the course while medicated, this is it. **Cardio does not substitute.**

**Total intake monitoring.** Under-eating drives tissue loss; the drug makes it effortless rather than causing it directly. Connects to Lesson 3 and Lesson 5 layers.

**Pre-taper preparation.** Given 6.5, establishing meal structure, appetite regulation, movement, and sleep habits **before** discontinuation is the highest-leverage use of the medicated window — appetite suppression makes habit formation easier now than it will be later.

**>>> FRAMING RULE:** position the course as what the medication cannot do. Never as an argument against it.

heading: 6.7 GI adverse events
text:
**[SUPPORTED]** Sodhi et al., *JAMA* 2023. Retrospective claims cohort, comparator bupropion-naltrexone. Approximate hazard ratios: pancreatitis 9.09, bowel obstruction 4.22, gastroparesis 3.67.

**>>> COACH RULE — NEVER QUOTE THE HAZARD RATIO ALONE.** These are large relative increases on low-incidence outcomes. Relative-only presentation materially overstates individual risk.

**>>> OPEN ITEM — absolute incidence rates not yet obtained.** Until they are: state that relative increases were substantial **and** that underlying rates were low in both groups, without quoting a specific multiple.

**Limitations to state if asked:** retrospective, claims-based, single comparator drug, potential residual confounding.

**Gastroparesis** is worth naming specifically — slowed gastric emptying is the therapeutic mechanism, and **it can persist after stopping.** *Verify before the coach states persistence.*

heading: 6.8 Gastric distension vs. nutrient-sensed satiety
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** Gastric stretch is detected by vagal mechanoreceptors — volume-dependent, nutrient-blind, dissipating within roughly 30–90 minutes. Nutrient-sensed satiety operates via CCK, GLP-1, and PYY and persists for hours.

**>>> COACH USE — very high frequency:** this is the answer to "I was full and hungry again an hour later," and it explains why volume-based strategies (large low-calorie volume, water preloading) underperform. They recruit the signal that fades and skip the one that lasts.

**Also the correct answer to "drink water, you're probably just thirsty"** — see Lesson 7 layer; that advice is poorly supported.

doc_subtitle: Coach reference — backend layer, not for direct user display
heading: 6.9 Pharmacological vs. physiological signalling
text:
**[ESTABLISHED]** GLP-1 agonists are engineered for DPP-4 resistance and albumin binding, producing half-lives of days against endogenous minutes, at supraphysiological concentrations. This is the design intent and the basis of weekly dosing.

**>>> COACH USE:** gives the course's critique a mechanism rather than an adjective — a meal-responsive signal versus a sustained constant. Accurate, non-pejorative, and it doesn't require overstating harm.

heading: 6.10 Natural GLP-1 support
text:
**[SUPPORTED]** Dietary: protein and fat as potent secretagogues; fermentable fibre via direct and SCFA-mediated routes; polyphenol-rich foods with more modest evidence. Lifestyle: exercise, adequate sleep, stress reduction, slower eating.

**>>> COACH RULE:** these produce physiological, not pharmacological, effects. **Do not imply equivalence to the medications** — the claim isn't supported and it would undermine credibility elsewhere. Defensible framing: these optimize your own system, which is a different goal than overriding it.

section: COMMON USER QUESTIONS FROM THIS LESSON
heading: COMMON USER QUESTIONS FROM THIS LESSON
text:
**"Should I stop taking it?"**

**That's a decision for you and your prescriber, and I'm not going to influence it either way.** What I can help with is protecting your muscle while you're on it, and getting you ready for whenever you do come off — because the research says that's the vulnerable moment.

**>>> Do not supply reasoning in either direction. Do not list drawbacks in response to this question.**

**"Am I losing muscle?"**

Possibly. Rapid weight loss of any kind costs lean tissue, and roughly a quarter to 40% of what comes off is typically lean — which is similar across methods, including dieting.

**What matters more is that it's largely preventable, and almost nobody is telling patients how.** Protein on a schedule, resistance training twice a week, and enough total food. Those three change the composition of what you lose substantially.

**And here's the useful part:** the real-world data shows it's **dose-dependent** — higher doses and longer use, more lean loss. That's worth raising with your prescriber, because it's something that can be adjusted.

**>>> Track strength, not the scale.** If you're lifting more than you were three months ago, you're not losing meaningful muscle regardless of what a scan says.

**"Which is worse, Ozempic or Mounjaro?"**

In the routine-care data, **tirzepatide showed more lean tissue loss than semaglutide at every point measured.** That's a real difference and it's a legitimate question for your prescriber — along with dose, since both drugs showed dose-dependent effects.

**>>> Do not recommend one over the other. Route to prescriber.**

**"Will I gain it all back if I stop?"**

The data isn't encouraging, and you should know it. In the follow-up study, participants regained about two-thirds of what they'd lost by two years, with most metabolic improvements drifting back toward baseline.

**That's not a willpower failure.** The drug was doing the appetite regulation. When it stops, appetite comes back — to a body that now has less muscle and lower energy needs.

**Which is exactly why the preparation matters.** Everything in this course is what you want in place *before* you taper. And it's much easier to build those habits now, while appetite suppression is working for you, than afterward when you're hungry.

**"I'm not hungry at all. Is that a problem?"**

It can be. **Appetite suppression is the mechanism — and it's also how people end up eating far less than they intended without deciding to.** Under-eating is what drives tissue loss.

Eat your protein on a schedule rather than waiting to want it. And if you've been eating noticeably less without choosing to, that's worth correcting.

**>>> Under gating: discuss qualitatively, no numbers.**

section: COMMON USER QUESTIONS FROM THIS LESSON
heading: COMMON USER QUESTIONS FROM THIS LESSON
text:
**"Can I get the same effect naturally?"**

Not the same effect — and I'd rather be straight with you than sell you something. The drugs work at concentrations your body never produces, sustained for days. Nothing you eat replicates that.

**What you can do is optimize your own system**, which is a different goal: protein and fat at every meal, fermentable fibre, eating slowly, sleeping properly, and not eating around the clock. Those produce real satiety signalling that lasts hours instead of minutes.

**>>> Never claim equivalence.**

**"Are the GI risks as bad as I've read?"**

The relative increases are large and real. **The absolute rates are low** — these are uncommon events becoming less uncommon, not common ones. Both numbers matter.

**Gastroparesis is the one I'd ask your doctor about specifically**, because slowing the stomach is how the drug works, and in some people it slows too much.
